name: ILM-TR

paper.title: Enhancing Long Context Performance in LLMs Through Inner Loop Query Mechanism
paper.venue: NeurIPS 2024 Workshop on Adaptive Foundation Models

construction.unit: tree node: raw chunk, chunk/cluster summary, or surprising-information text
construction.kept_as: leaves verbatim; summaries and surprising facts written by the LLM
construction.processing: chunk (≤600 tokens), LLM writes a summary plus a list of surprising facts; GMM clusters the summaries and each cluster is summarized again, recursively (RAPTOR-style)
construction.writer: Meta-Llama-3-70B (Q4_K_M, llama.cpp) as summary model; SBERT multi-qa-mpnet-base-cos-v1 embeddings

organization.structure: RAPTOR tree of recursive summaries, with surprising-information nodes beside each summary
organization.stores: one tree per document, searched as a flat table; Short-Term Memory (STM) text buffer at query time

management.operations: STM overwritten with the answer model's new output each inner-loop round

retrieval.query: user query plus current STM text
retrieval.candidates: collapsed tree: every node of every level in one table
retrieval.selection: nearest by vector distance (top-k not stated)
retrieval.budget: not stated; up to 5 inner-loop rounds

use.reasoning: repeat retrieve-then-write until STM stops changing (LCS check) or 5 rounds; final STM is the answer

classify.note: The document tree is append-only; what is updated in place is the STM buffer, which the answer LLM rewrites each round and which is fed back into the next query.

stages.ingestion: The long input is split into contiguous chunks of at most 600 tokens; a sentence that would cross the limit moves to the next chunk.
stages.construction: The summary model writes, per chunk, a regular summary and a separate list of surprising facts that differ from the main text.
stages.organization: As in RAPTOR, summaries (not surprising facts) are embedded with SBERT, clustered with Gaussian mixtures and summarized again, recursively, into a multi-level tree.
stages.update: At query time a Short-Term Memory (STM) holds up to the answer model's output length; each inner-loop round overwrites it with the new answer text.
stages.retrieval: Collapsed-tree search: all nodes sit in one table and the closest by vector distance to the query (question plus current STM) are returned.
stages.answer: The answer model reads retrieved info, the previous STM and the question and writes a new STM; the loop stops when STM converges (LCS) or after 5 rounds, and the STM is returned as the answer.

summary: RAPTOR-style summary tree whose nodes also keep 'surprising' facts, read by an inner loop that re-queries the tree with the LLM's own intermediate answer (Short-Term Memory) until it stops changing.
notes:
Long-context QA paper (4-page NeurIPS 2024 AFM workshop paper); memory is a document tree plus a query-time scratch buffer, not a conversational store. Results are heatmaps on M-NIAH and BABILong with 10 test cases per cell; there is no official code link in the paper and no repository was found by name search.
DESIGN: §3, §4, App. A.1-A.3.

sources.code_note: No code link in the paper; a GitHub search for ILM-TR and the full method name found no repository. Top-k, retrieved-token budget and the LCS convergence threshold are not stated (App. A.3 says unlisted parameters are defaults).

abstract.text: ILM-TR targets long inputs that exceed the model's context window. It builds a RAPTOR-like tree of chunk and cluster summaries, but asks the summarizer to also list surprising facts that do not fit the main content. At question time an inner loop retrieves from the tree, lets the LLM write an intermediate answer into a small Short-Term Memory, and uses that memory together with the question as the next query, until the memory stops changing. With Llama-3-70B the authors report finding all needles in a multi-needle test up to 500k tokens and gains over RAPTOR on BABILong.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: Two changes to RAPTOR: summaries also list 'surprising' facts, and retrieval loops, feeding the LLM's own intermediate answer back into the query.
The Short-Term Memory is a single ≤200-token text that is overwritten each round and returned as the final answer.
Results are 10 test cases per heatmap cell with a 4-bit Llama-3-70B; no top-k or context budget is given.

units.name: Tree node
units.role: one searchable text in the collapsed tree

fields.name: summary
fields.what: summary of a chunk or of a cluster of summaries (≤300 tokens)

fields.name: surprising information
fields.what: facts in the text that differ from its main content; not clustered

fields.name: STM
fields.what: latest intermediate answer, up to the answer model's max output (200 tokens)

write.how: one LLM call per chunk returns '(Summary)' and '(Surprise)' parts
GMM over SBERT embeddings of summaries only; each cluster summarized again with its own surprise part; repeat until clustering is impractical

read.input: question (STM empty in round 1), later question + STM

read.how: answer LLM reads retrieved info, previous STM and question; may write partial reasoning ('we need to find ...')
compare STM across rounds with longest common subsequence; stop when it stops changing or at the query limit

answer_context.sees: retrieved tree nodes, the previous STM and the question
answer_context.format: '(Retrieved Info):' ... '(Memory):' ... '(Question):' with a few-shot example (App. A.1.2)

compression.basis: STM is capped at the answer model's max output (max_tokens 200, App. A.3); longest M-NIAH input 500k tokens (§4)
Not reported: top-k and retrieved-token budget are not given.

numbers.label: M-NIAH cells with all 3 needles (40 cells)
numbers.src: paper Fig. 3 (our count of cell colours)

open_questions: The retrieval budget is not given, so it is unknown how much text the answer model sees per round and whether the loop gains come from reading more nodes over 5 rounds.
The no-loop ablation still uses surprise summaries; there is no run of RAPTOR plus the loop without surprise summaries, so the two changes are separated in one direction only.

text: The question plus the Short-Term Memory is used to search the whole tree; the answer LLM rewrites the STM from what it finds.
The loop repeats until the STM stops changing or after 5 rounds, and the STM itself is returned as the answer.

ablation.src: paper Fig. 3 (our count of cell colours) and Fig. 4 (printed cell values, % of 10 cases)

discussion.takeaway: Letting the LLM's intermediate answer steer further retrieval, and keeping surprising facts in the summaries, helps a RAPTOR tree find several scattered needles in very long inputs.

claims.claim: Adding surprising information to summaries improves multi-needle retrieval.
claims.evidence: M-NIAH: RAPTOR finds no needle in any of the 40 cells, ILM-TR without the loop finds all three in 23 and two in 13 (150k-500k tokens). §4, Fig. 3

claims.claim: The inner loop finds all needles.
claims.evidence: M-NIAH: all 40 cells score 10 up to 500k tokens. Fig. 3(c)

claims.claim: ILM-TR beats the RAPTOR baseline on BABILong.
claims.evidence: e.g. qa1 at 128k: 60 vs 0; qa5 at 64k: 70 vs 20 (10 cases per cell). Fig. 4

claims.claim: No major loss as context grows to 500k tokens.

limits: The inner loop needs several iterations, so answering takes longer.
Writing surprise summaries needs a model that follows complex instructions; 7-8B models failed the prompt, so a slower 70B model was used.
reading: Each heatmap cell has only 10 test cases (BABILong) and M-NIAH cells are shown by colour only, so small differences are within noise; our M-NIAH counts are read from colours.
The loop's gain on BABILong is mixed: ILM-TR is below its no-loop variant in some cells (qa2 at 8k 10 vs 20, qa4 at 64k 70 vs 80, qa5 at 32k 60 vs 70) and above in others.

The RAPTOR baseline uses a plain summary prompt and a plain answer prompt, while ILM-TR's no-loop variant changes only the summary prompt, so the no-loop variant isolates the surprise-summary change and the full system isolates the loop.
Retrieval top-k and token budget are not reported; the final answer is the STM text, which can still hold intermediate reasoning (App. A.2.2), and the BABILong scoring rule is not stated.
M-NIAH uses three needles on one topic (pizza ingredients) inserted into a haystack whose source text is not named.
